title: Is This The Conservative View Of Education?
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene responds to a Washington Times piece by Jay Greene of the Heritage Foundation, which contrasts a progressive view of education as workforce shaping with a conservative view that education should cultivate virtue and human dignity. Peter Greene argues that sorting education ideas into political team labels is a snare, noting that many self-described conservatives, from Rex Tillerson to A Nation at Risk, framed students as products for employers. He credits one sharp passage about coders and corporate demands but accuses the author of a No True Scotsman move to exclude conservatives who do not fit. He observes that the school choice coalition has shifted from free marketeers plus social-justice allies to a culture-war framing built around traditional virtue. His own constant is that each new argument for choice leaves the goalposts in place, which he reads as dismantling and privatizing public education. The post is policy commentary on the shifting rhetoric of the school choice movement.
points: The conservative-virtue versus progressive-industry framing is rebutted as a team-label exercise that cannot account for conservatives who championed workforce-driven schooling.
Greene highlights the claim that corporate demands for coders should not dictate how children are educated as the strongest passage in the piece he is answering.
Common Core and corporate reform show that every major education debate has supporters across the political spectrum, so left-right sorting is largely futile.
The case against choice has been reargued across decades (failing schools, national security, efficiency, rescue, freedom, now virtue) while the goal stayed constant.
His own stance is stated plainly: he cares about the fate of public education more than the logo on his jersey.
quotes: They begin with the belief that all human beings possess dignity — are created in the image of God, if you will. The purpose of education from this perspective is to cultivate and develop human dignity to serve what is sacred.

That whole construction is doing a lot of heavy, heavy lifting, some of which is wrapped up in the business of assigning team labels to particular ideas, which is never one of my favorite things. "To which team label shall we ascribe this idea" is far less interesting to me than "Is this idea any good.

Big companies that hire large numbers of coders naturally want the education system to increase its supply of coders, but it is unclear why their desires should determine how we educate our children. This is especially true as companies frequently use the fresh supply of newly trained and cheaper coders to replace the older and more expensive people they are laying off. Corporate executives may similarly want there to be more finishing schools to increase the supply of trophy wives to replace their older spouses, but we do not cater to their every whim.

Public education is not meant to serve the needs of employers, but the needs of students. Yes, students probably need a job. But a job training system is meager and narrow. Our children should aspire to more than being useful meat widgets.

Attempting to make the various threads of education reform line up with political identities is largely a snare and delusion. Almost anywhere you build your fence, you'll find a mix of people on all sides, so why bother to try?

Choice is necessary to restore traditional virtues. It will run until the next argument shows up. Choicers keep changing the game and the playing field, but the goalposts actually stay right where they've always been--dismantle and privatize education.
